parts.transcript: Today we’re pleased to have on the show Fatima Johnson, who is the organiser of the Adbourne Film Festival. Welcome, Fatima. Hello. Can you tell us a bit about the background to the festival and what it brings to the town? Well, the festival was started in 1996 by the then Mayor of Adbourne, Joanne Smith. She wasn’t a filmmaker herself. She’d actually been a very energetic tourism development officer for many years, but Adbourne had run a classical music festival which had been becoming less and less popular in recent years. Joanne was looking around for something to replace it and to use funds allocated to it to promote something which local people can enjoy. Great. So, tell us about the festival nowadays. Well, it’s held in the last two weeks of August every year, and short films from all over the world are shown in three places, in the theatre and our two cinemas. Several films are shown in one performance, and the whole thing lasts about 90 minutes. Tickets are very reasonably priced. Under twelves used to get in for 50p, but now we charge just one pound, which is still very good value! One pound fifty for students and two pounds fifty for everyone else. Performances are advertised all around town and also on our website www.adbournefest.com. If you’re interested in attending any performances, you can buy tickets online, of course, and you can also get them in the library, which is right next to the main shopping area. I’m afraid this year, tickets are no longer available from either of the two cinemas because of restricted opening times. I understand you also run a film competition? Yes, for under 18s. We have a different theme every year. Last year, for example, the theme was ‘Future Planet’ and the winner was a ten-minute documentary encouraging youngsters to be more aware of environmental issues, focusing on getting school kids to cycle to school instead of going by car. This year, the theme is ‘Sporting Nation’, so there’ll also be lots of ideas to choose from. Now we’re always on the lookout for new local talent, so if you live in the Adbourne area and are under 18, you should have a go. We have an excellent prize every year, donated by local businesses, shops, hotels, etc. This year, you can win a hi-spec movie camera worth over 800 pounds. Application forms are on the website, and the deadline for sending in your film to enter the competition is the last day of July. It’s May now, so you’ll have the whole of June to be working on it. And what are the judges looking for? Well, although we choose very topical issues like the environment, we’re not looking for propaganda, you know, trying to get people to do something. Instead, we’re looking for a new angle, a fresh way of looking at a theme. And of course, because it’s a short-film festival, it’s not really about a fully worked story with well-rounded characters. It’s more about good photography, conveying things visually. And who judges the films? A panel of three people who know a lot about film. We’ve used the same judges for many years, and we’re very happy with their expertise. One thing we probably will change next year, though, is that we want to add another class and another prize for older filmmakers. We’ll keep it at a maximum of ten minutes, though; the length works well for our festival. We also want to use different venues for the film shows, such as community centres and at least one school. It might make performances more accessible to a wider audience. We did explore the possibility of having late-night showings, but that’s unlikely to happen in the coming year. So, as I say, if anyone’s interested in submitting a film for our competition, go onto our website, and you’ll be able to access everything…

We're lucky to have a double-free period today, so we will have plenty of time to revise this together. Okay. Next up is Mount Fago. This is an ancient mythical volcano, the location of which is unclear. There are mountainous regions in both Mexico and the USA, both of which are rumored to be the site of this volcano. It's not very scientific to list two separate locations for one volcano. But since no one has been able to prove which is the correct one, we're left with no choice. It's interesting that there is no other example of a volcano in existence today that is surrounded by so much mystery. Absolutely. I think we should include some information about Mount Etna in Sicily, which is famous for the stunning panoramas that one can appreciate from its peak. According to Google, it's a relatively new volcano compared to others in the surrounding region, which may be why it has very few of the features found in older volcanoes. Oh, how interesting. Shall we include information on Mount Herton? I don't think that any of the other students have carried out much research into it, even though it has a lot of unique features. parts.transcript: Good afternoon, everybody. And in our second talk on social psychology, I want to look at the role of laughter in our lives, something that usually gets everyone smiling from the start. So, first of all, I’ll start by looking at the actual nature of laughter. Well, when someone laughs, you’ve got movement of the muscles of the face and the chest, and you’ve got sound formed when the air’s forced out of the body as part of this process, so we’re talking about a physical activity. But obviously, other things are involved as well, and this is where it gets more complicated. Laughing isn’t something that you normally decide to do, so it’s not voluntary behavior, like ordinary speech. Instead, it’s regulated by our instincts, rather like the singing of a bird or the roaring of a lion. And once you start to laugh, it can be quite hard to stop. That’s not always under your conscious control, either. But why do we laugh? Because we find something funny, most of us would say. But in fact, it appears that laughter has little to do with jokes or funny stories. Only about 10 percent of laughter is caused by things like that. One suggestion is that human laughter may have originally started out as a shared response to signal relief at the passing of danger. And it’s true that, even these days, laughter's rarely an activity carried out by an individual on his or her own. In fact, people are 30 times more likely to laugh when they’re with other people than when they’re completely alone. Laughter still seems to be a kind of social signal; it occurs when people are in a group, and they’re comfortable with one another. And it seems likely that laughter can result in the creation of bonds between the people in the group. And it’s precisely because of this social aspect of laughter that people like public speakers and politicians often try to get their audience to laugh. It encourages their listeners to trust them and to connect with them. But this kind of thing, controlling the laughter of a group, that is, indicates that there’s a link between laughter and power, and this is supported by several studies that indicate that bosses use humor more than their employees. And research has also shown that female listeners are likely to laugh much more if the speaker is male, so it appears that there are gender issues associated with how much we laugh. I should also point out that laughter can be used as a negative signal as well as a positive one. I think we’ve all probably seen evidence of a group using laughter to exclude someone, to emphasize that they are not accepted. So it’s not always a positive type of behavior, either. So what all this goes to show is that laughter is a very, very complex issue. It does appear, however, that laughter has definite benefits. If we look first at the psychological aspects, we know that people often tend to store negative emotions, such as anger, sadness, and fear, rather than expressing them, and it seems that laughter provides a harmless way for the release of these emotions. But there are also clear physical effects that have been monitored, too. For example, laughter is good aerobic exercise. It speeds up heart rate and respiration, and raises blood pressure. One researcher suggests that 100 laughs a day is the equivalent of 10 minutes’ jogging. Laughter also helps prevent the stress that so many people suffer from today, which results from the faster pace of life and all that goes with it. One interesting study showed that people who had had surgical operations asked for fewer painkillers if they’d been viewing comic films. Laughter still seems to be a kind of social signal; it occurs when people are in a group, and they’re comfortable with one another. And it seems likely that laughter can result in the creation of bonds between the people in the group. And it’s precisely because of this social aspect of laughter that people like public speakers and politicians often try to get their audience to laugh. It encourages their listeners to trust them and to connect with them. But this kind of thing, controlling the laughter of a group, that is, indicates that there’s a link between laughter and power, and this is supported by several studies that indicate that bosses use humor more than their employees. And research has also shown that female listeners are likely to laugh much more if the speaker is male, so it appears that there are gender issues associated with how much we laugh. I should also point out that laughter can be used as a negative signal as well as a positive one. I think we’ve all probably seen evidence of a group using laughter to exclude someone, to emphasize that they are not accepted. So it’s not always a positive type of behavior, either. So what all this goes to show is that laughter is a very, very complex issue. It does appear, however, that laughter has definite benefits. If we look first at the psychological aspects, we know that people often tend to store negative emotions, such as anger, sadness, and fear, rather than expressing them, and it seems that laughter provides a harmless way for the release of these emotions. But there are also clear physical effects that have been monitored, too. For example, laughter is good aerobic exercise. It speeds up heart rate and respiration, and raises blood pressure. One researcher suggests that 100 laughs a day is the equivalent of 10 minutes’ jogging. Laughter also helps prevent the stress that so many people suffer from today, which results from the faster pace of life and all that goes with it. It does this by reducing the levels of hormones in the blood which are caused by stress. And, in addition, it is known to increase the levels of chemicals that protect the body from infection or pain and so it helps to boost the immune system. One interesting study showed that people who had had surgical operations asked for fewer painkillers if they’d been viewing comic films. In fact, research has even shown that the quality of dreams can be positively affected by laughter. A good laugh 10 minutes before going to sleep can prevent you from having bad dreams and give a much more pleasant and restorative night’s sleep. So, there’s now little argument that finding things funny and enjoying a good laugh is extremely beneficial to us all. The Horizon Newspaper Travel Writing Competition

We are thrilled to announce the return of our annual travel writing competition, offering you the chance to win a once-in-a-lifetime travel assignment in Finnish Lapland.

Are you passionate about exploring new places and sharing your stories? If so, our annual travel writing competition, run by the Travel section of The Horizon Newspaper, is for you. This competition is your platform to chronicle your journeys—whether they take you across the globe or just around the corner.

Each month will feature a new travel theme. Our travel writing team, joined by a special guest author, will select one winner whose article will be published on The Horizon Newspaper website.

Every monthly winner will receive:

A £200 travel voucher to fund your next adventure.

An exclusive, leather-bound Horizon journal.

Inclusion in our special end-of-year digital anthology showcasing all 12 winning pieces.

To ensure a fair playing field for our readers, this competition is exclusively open to amateur writers who have not previously worked as professional journalists or published authors. Entrants must be legal residents of the UK at the time of submission.

The Grand Prize: Finnish Lapland

At the end of the year, our judging panel will select one Grand Prize winner from the 12 monthly finalists.

The overall winner will embark on a spectacular four-night trip to Finnish Lapland. Every part of the trip is designed to give you rich, first-hand material for your very own travel feature. Guided by local experts, you will immerse yourself in the region’s breathtaking winter landscapes, rich culture, and exhilarating outdoor pursuits.

Your trip includes:

Return flights from the UK.

Four nights of premium accommodation with full board.

Specialist cold-weather clothing and wilderness equipment for the duration of the trip.

Excursions led by fully qualified wilderness guides.

One-on-one editorial support and mentoring from The Horizon travel team.

As the Grand Prize winner, you will be commissioned to write a feature article about your Lapland experience to be published in the print and digital Travel sections of The Horizon Newspaper. To ensure the visual storytelling matches your writing, you will either be provided with a high-quality digital camera for the duration of the trip or be accompanied by a professional Horizon staff photographer.

(Please note: The Horizon Newspaper reserves the right to edit the final article as necessary for publication. The winner will receive a full byline alongside their published work.)

passages.title: Section 2: Types of Training in Business
passages.passageHtml:
Types of Training in Business

The type of training a business provides is influenced by several factors, including the resources it can devote to employee development, the nature of its operations and the priority placed on training by senior management. Although training may require an initial investment of time and money, it can improve productivity, reduce costly errors and help employees adapt more effectively to their roles.

One common category is technical training, which equips employees with the technological knowledge required to perform their work. In a logistics company, for example, warehouse operatives may need instruction in using scanning systems to register incoming and outgoing stock accurately. Hotel receptionists, meanwhile, are often trained to manage reservations through property-management software. As many businesses increasingly rely on digital systems, technical training must also be updated whenever new equipment or software is introduced.

Quality training is particularly important in organisations centred on manufacturing or production. Its purpose is to familiarise employees with methods of preventing, identifying and eliminating goods that fail to meet the required standards. Staff may be taught how to inspect raw materials, recognise defects and report recurring problems before large quantities of faulty products are produced. Since quality can distinguish one company from its competitors, employees must understand both the standards they are expected to maintain and the action to take when those standards are not met. Effective quality training can reduce waste, returns, and repair costs while also protecting the company’s reputation. Consistently high standards may therefore provide an edge in the marketing of the product.

Skills training focuses on the practical abilities needed to carry out the job itself. A hairdresser, for instance, may receive instruction in different colouring techniques, whereas a bank employee might learn how to explain loan options clearly and guide customers through the application process. Similarly, a barista must know not only how to operate coffee-making equipment but also what procedures to follow when an order has been prepared incorrectly. This kind of training often includes demonstrations, supervised practice and feedback, allowing employees to improve their performance before working independently.

Another important category is soft-skills training. Soft skills are the personal qualities and habits that influence how effectively individuals interact with others. Employers increasingly seek staff who combine technical competence with strong communication and interpersonal skills, such as attentive listening and collaboration. In healthcare and travel settings, employees may also need to demonstrate empathy, remain composed under pressure and reassure anxious clients. These abilities are especially valuable when dealing with complaints or other emotionally demanding situations. Because soft skills shape almost every interaction with colleagues and customers, they play a central role in teamwork, customer satisfaction and the overall reputation of a business.

passages.title: Section 3: The Importance of Business Cards
passages.passageHtml:
The Importance of Business Cards

The exchange of business cards is as close to a universal ritual as you can find in the business world.

The ritual may be universal, but the details of business cards and how they are swapped vary across countries. Americans throw their cards casually across a table; the Japanese make the exchange of cards a formal ceremony. While there are cards that are discreet and understated, others are crammed full of details and titles. Some businesspeople hand out 24-carat gold cards, and there are kindergarten children who have cards with not only their own contact details, but also with the job descriptions of their parents and even grandparents. This practice has become so common in parts of New York, for example, that the use of such cards is now prohibited by some kindergartens.

Cards have been around a long time in one form or another. The Chinese invented calling cards in the 15th century to give people notice that they intended to pay them a visit, but these were for social purposes only. Then, in the 17th century, European businesspeople invented a new type of card to act as miniature advertisements, signalling the advent of the business card. In today’s world, business cards can cause people to have strong emotional reactions. According to one experienced company director, very few things can provoke more heated discussion at a board meeting than the composition of the company’s business cards.

Lots of companies try to promote themselves by altering the form of the card. Employees at one famous toy company give out little plastic figures with their contact details stamped on them. One fast-food company has business cards which are shaped like a portion of French fries. A Canadian divorce lawyer once gave out cards that could be torn in two – one half for each of the spouses. For many business commentators, such gimmicky business cards prove that the use of a physical business card is nearly at an end. After all, why bother exchanging bits of thick paper at all when you can simply swap electronic versions by smartphone?

However, one can just as well argue the opposite: that business cards are here to stay, and, in a business world full of meetings and correspondence, it is more important than ever that your card is unique. Attempts to reinvent business cards for the digital age have not been successful. Digital options may include QR codes that open an online profile or smartphone apps that transfer contact details instantly between devices, without requiring a printed card. Yet even at the latest technology conferences, people still greet each other by handing out little rectangles made from paper rather than using a digital alternative.

To understand business cards, it is necessary to understand how business works. That business cards are thriving in a digital age is a forceful reminder that there is much about business that is timeless. According to Kate Jones, a business lecturer, there is one eternal and inescapable issue. Her 2006 study of more than 200 business executives in North America found that trust was the key element for running a successful business. It is vital to look someone in the eye and decide what sort of person they are. Such personal contact can transform acquaintanceships into relationships over the longer term.

A good proportion of business life will always involve building social connections, such as having dinner or playing sports with clients and colleagues. While computers can deal with administrative tasks, human beings must manage the emotional side. The advance of globalization makes this harder: managers put more effort into dealings with international counterparts, especially when they do not share a language. A UK survey found that global chief executives routinely spend three out of every four weeks on international travel. In these situations, cards quickly establish connections and strengthen memory of face-to-face meetings in a way that uniform electronic lists cannot.

Janet McIntyre, a leading expert on business cards today, maintains that as companies become more complex, cards are essential in showing the exact status of contacts in multinational corporations. Exchanging them is also an effective way of initiating a conversation, since it provides a ritual when people first meet. The business world is obsessed with creating and inventing new things that will change how we work, and such innovation does lead to progress. Nevertheless, Janet argues that some practices do not need to be changed, and that tradition has an equally valuable role. The exchange of business cards is therefore likely to continue.

I look forward to receiving your prompt resolution.

task2.title: Task 2: General Essay
task2.prompt: In many countries today, people are spending less time with their families and more time at work or pursuing individual hobbies. What are the causes of this trend, and what effects does it have on society?
task2.sampleBand8Answer:
In contemporary society, an increasing number of individuals devote an overwhelming proportion of their daily lives to workplace commitments and autonomous pastimes, resulting in a noticeable decline in familial interaction. This essay will examine the primary catalysts behind this phenomenon and discuss its profound ramifications for community cohesion.

The primary impetus behind diminishing family time is escalating economic pressure and the competitive nature of the globalized job market. With housing costs and general living expenses soaring in metropolitan hubs, adults frequently find themselves obliged to work excessive overtime or manage secondary freelance gigs to attain financial stability. Concurrently, the pervasive presence of personalized digital entertainment—such as algorithmic social media and on-demand streaming—encourages solitary engagement rather than collective domestic pastimes.

Regarding the impacts, this societal transition generates considerable adverse repercussions. Within the household, the lack of parental presence and meaningful communication can weaken intergenerational bonding, leaving children vulnerable to behavioral issues and emotional isolation. At a broader societal level, the erosion of cohesive family structures diminishes the collective resilience of communities, as strong domestic units have traditionally served as the initial safety net during psychological and financial crises.

In summary, intense corporate demands and digital individualism represent the chief reasons why people are drifting from domestic life. Unless societies institute sustainable work-life balance policies, familial ties and social well-being will continue to erode.
